author: Claude (EFL materials writer role)
basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.

slides.1: Our education system looks excellent on paper, but does it actually give every student the same chance? Today I want to test that question through the subject I know best: science.
slides.2: The fourth goal promises inclusive, lifelong learning. It should not matter what your family earns or where you live. Taiwan built a high-tech economy on that promise, yet we rarely ask whether our tools are ethical.
slides.3: Taiwan has poured money into STEM for decades, and that investment built our growth. Now the birth rate has hit a record low. We should ask whether those resources still reach the problems that matter most.
slides.4: Births have collapsed from 300,000 in 1990 to under 140,000 last year. Because of this, rural schools are shutting, and the students left behind must travel much further.
slides.5: In science lessons we spend our time memorizing answers for the exam, and creativity quietly disappears. Students who might have loved research drop it early. Will that habit help us solve something like climate change?
slides.6: City classrooms have modern laboratories, while remote schools share what little equipment they own. Official surveys put that resource gap at roughly 30%. Is our system built to close it, or to ignore it?
slides.7: Now for the achievements. Our 12 years of basic schooling cost families nothing, and 99% of children complete primary education. That puts us at the top of the OECD range, though access has never meant quality.
slides.8: Early-years policy is stronger. Government subsidies now put 96% of disadvantaged five-year-olds into preschool, where they pick up the counting and questioning that later science depends on. The gap starts to narrow before school even starts.
slides.9: Our enrollment and graduation rates beat the global average, and better teacher training has improved what happens in the classroom. Yet high participation can hide how differently our regions actually teach.
slides.10: The response has started. Public money is now going into inquiry-based STEM courses, so a lesson means building something rather than reading about it. Children meet coding and AI ethics far earlier than we did.
slides.11: More than 80% of our schools now run digital lessons. Simulations let a class experiment without a laboratory, which links the classroom to our semiconductor industry. But students still need to learn responsible use.
slides.12: Programs for talented students place them inside technology firms for real projects. They work beside engineers in renewable energy, so the distance between a textbook and a career suddenly shrinks.
slides.13: Science education feeds an export economy worth around 500 billion US dollars annually. The same knowledge also builds the climate-resilient infrastructure that a hotter, wetter island will need.
slides.14: Not everything has improved: women still take only 30% of engineering degrees, and the old idea that technology suits men has never quite died. Those stereotypes cost talent we cannot spare.
slides.15: If we ignore these gaps, inequality will deepen and a whole generation of talent is wasted. As college students we should ask whether policy can keep pace with AI-driven work.
slides.16: Education decides how resilient a society can be. Without serious reform, though, Taiwan will slowly lose its edge in sustainable technology. Our science teaching has to keep evolving alongside the century that it serves.
slides.17: In summary, SDG 4 shows both real progress and stubborn problems. STEM has been the engine of our development, and enrollment is high. But we still have to make the system fair for every learner.
slides.18: Our test scores look impressive internationally, yet they measure memory far better than imagination or fairness. Real reform means changing what we reward, not adding another examination to the calendar.
slides.19: In future, inclusive STEM must reach the groups we usually overlook, and our curriculum needs an update. Every course should connect what it teaches to something happening outside the classroom window.
slides.20: Here is the ask. Join the debate about school policy, volunteer where rural classrooms need help, or push your own department to change its curriculum. Taiwan can create an education system that leaves no one out.
